name: Training Data and Opt-Outs
title: Training Data and Opt-Outs
answer: Training data and opt-outs covers the sources used to teach generative image, video, and audio models, and the ways creators can ask that their work be excluded. It includes scraped web images, licensed archives, commissioned shoots, public domain collections, synthetic outputs, and the metadata that records where each item came from. It also covers the practical meaning of an opt-out, whether that is a platform setting, a robots.txt signal, a contract clause, or a removal request after training has already happened. The site tracks 1000 live image generation models, and each one may rest on a different mix of these sources, so the scope is both technical and contractual.

sections.body: Training data and opt-outs covers the sources used to teach generative image, video, and audio models, and the ways creators can ask that their work be excluded. It includes scraped web images, licensed archives, commissioned shoots, public domain collections, synthetic outputs, and the metadata that records where each item came from. It also covers the practical meaning of an opt-out, whether that is a platform setting, a robots.txt signal, a contract clause, or a removal request after training has already happened. The site tracks 1000 live image generation models, and each one may rest on a different mix of these sources, so the scope is both technical and contractual.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on large storage and compute clusters that hold and process image, video, and audio datasets, often in object stores with indexed metadata. Training pipelines read from these stores, apply filters and captions, and feed batches to GPUs or other accelerators. Opt-out systems run alongside as registries, crawler rules, hashing services, and rights databases that must be checked before or during data collection. Provenance tools such as C2PA manifests and dataset cards may also sit in this layer, linking a model or output back to source records.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: In practice, teams assemble a dataset by crawling or licensing content, then clean, deduplicate, caption, and filter it before training. Opt-outs are handled through several channels, including crawler exclusion files, platform preference flags, direct artist requests, and contractual restrictions negotiated with rights holders. Because removal after training is difficult, some teams keep source-level records so they can retrain or filter later if a claim arises. Others use similarity search or membership tests to find whether a specific work influenced a model, though these methods are imperfect and often contested.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The governance question is who bears the risk when training data is collected without clear consent, and how provenance is documented from source to model to output. Opt-out mechanisms vary widely, and an artist who blocks one crawler may still find their work in a dataset obtained from another source. The site counts 92 active intellectual property lawsuits, 18 of which involve AI music services, which shows how quickly these disputes move from policy debate into court. Common measures include dataset documentation, license review, and a process for handling takedown or exclusion requests, and this page describes practice rather than giving legal advice.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward more granular opt-outs, better provenance records, and clearer separation between licensed, public domain, and scraped material. Standards for content credentials and dataset transparency are likely to become more common, though adoption will be uneven across image, video, and audio models. Expect more tools that let creators register exclusion preferences once and have them checked by multiple data collectors, and more pressure to make retraining and removal feasible. The legal picture will keep shifting as courts and regulators respond to the active intellectual property lawsuits tracked on this site, and both technical standards and case law remain moving targets.
